sections.html:
Middlesex County sits in central New Jersey, from the Raritan Valley toward the northern end of the Jersey Shore, with New Brunswick as the county seat. The county government counts twenty-five municipalities. Edison is the largest, with 107,588 residents in 2020, and Monroe Township covers the most ground at 42.19 square miles. Other towns include Woodbridge, East Brunswick, Perth Amboy, South Amboy, South Brunswick, Metuchen and South Plainfield.

A house in a Raritan Bay town such as South Amboy and one in a Route 1 corridor township such as South Brunswick are billed by different municipalities and school districts, even though the same county board rules on their appeals.

Middlesex County does not send most homeowners a tax bill. In each of the twenty-five towns, a local assessor values property and a local collector sends the bill, and the county tax board supervises that work and hears appeals. Your town's collector is the person to ask for payment help and payoff numbers.

The Middlesex County Board of Taxation is the county office:

  • Location: County Administration Building, 4th Floor, 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick, NJ 08901.
  • Phone: 732-745-3350. The office opens weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:15 PM.
  • Duties: certifying assessments and municipal tax rates, equalizing assessments for county taxes, preparing the abstract of ratables, supervising local assessors and hearing appeals.

Five commissioners sit on the Middlesex board, and the county tax administrator runs the daily office. County tax boards date from legislation in 1909, and all 21 of them follow one set of rules written by the state Division of Taxation.

The board needs your petition in hand by April 1, or 45 days after assessment notices are mailed in bulk, if that is later. A town that finished a revaluation or reassessment moves the date to May 1. The January 15 calendar used in a few other counties does not apply here.

How filing works:

  • Create an account on the board's online portal, file there, and save the proof of filing the portal issues.
  • The board sends the petition on to your assessor and clerk.
  • Upload evidence with the petition or as late as seven calendar days before the hearing, by 4:00 PM.
  • Appeals of added and omitted assessments are due each year on a separate December 1 date.
  • The board holds no virtual hearings, so plan to attend in person or send your evidence ahead.

You are disputing the assessment only, since local budgets set the taxes. The test is the common level range, plus or minus 15% of the director's ratio for the town. Under the freeze act, an appealed value holds for the assessment year and the next two years unless something changes the property.

The county estimate for July 2025 is 883,335 residents. Owners occupy 63.6% of homes, the median home value is $462,900, median household income is $111,549 and median gross rent is $1,871. County-wide density is 2,791.4 people per square mile on 309.22 square miles of land.

More than a third of households rent, so condominiums and multifamily properties sit alongside single-family houses, and many buyers commute by rail or turnpike. Several stations on NJ Transit's Northeast Corridor Line serve the county, and the Turnpike and Parkway meet in Woodbridge. Wet summers and freezing winters are normal here, so roofs, gutters and basements are routine items on a buyer's inspection list.

sections.h2: Unpaid property tax when you sell
sections.html:
Your first call goes to your own town's collector, since the county never collects. Request a payoff in writing that runs through the day you expect to close, and find out whether the town has sold a lien on the parcel. You owe the tax whether or not a bill reached you, and installments fall at the start of February, May, August and November.

Planning an appeal? The April 1 date (May 1 after a revaluation) still applies, and the first quarter's taxes and municipal charges normally have to be paid for it to move forward. Questions about a pending petition go to the county tax board at 732-745-3350. A reduction can change the value a buyer sees on the record.

Calling the wrong office wastes a week, so match the question to the desk. The town assessor explains the value on your record, the collector explains the balance, and the county board reports where a petition stands. Once the deed is recorded, the buyer's name reaches the assessor and later bills follow the new owner. Clear any open quarter before then so the buyer takes over a clean account.

A lien sold on your parcel is a claim that must be paid, with interest, before the title is clear. Get the redemption amount from the collector in writing. The title company will also ask for the block and lot number printed on your bill, so keep it handy.

The steps before a closing are short:

  • Call your town's collector for a payoff that runs through the closing date.
  • Ask about liens and any water or sewer balance that sits outside the tax account.
  • Give the written figure to the title company so it is paid from your proceeds.

A cash buyer can close quickly, but the same payoff and lien check applies before the deed is recorded.

The state's Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ programs are three separate benefits with a yearly application window, so check the Division of Taxation relief page for the next one. Relief also changes with a sale, so ask the program office how a move affects your claim. Local senior, disabled and veteran deductions go through your town's assessor, and the assessor can tell you what the new owner must file.

If you inherited the house, check whether a deduction that belonged to the former owner is still on the account. The deduction ends when the owner who qualified no longer lives there, and the assessor can tell you what to file so the next bill is correct. Do this before you list, since buyers and their lenders look at the bill on record when they estimate monthly costs.

Whatever program you use, keep the confirmation letters. A title company may ask for proof that a deduction or credit was removed or transferred, and a letter from the assessor or the state office settles that question quickly.

faqs.q: Where does a Middlesex County owner send an assessment petition?
faqs.a: File with the Middlesex County Board of Taxation, which accepts petitions online and at 75 Bayard Street, New Brunswick. Each petition is passed on to the municipal assessor and clerk.

faqs.q: What is the standard appeal deadline in Middlesex County?
faqs.a: April 1, or within 45 days after bulk-mailed assessment notices, with May 1 for towns that completed a revaluation or reassessment. Added and omitted assessment appeals follow a separate December 1 date.

faqs.q: Does Middlesex County collect my property taxes?
faqs.a: No. Your municipal tax collector mails the bill and accepts the payment, and the county board of taxation supervises assessments and hears appeals. Contact the collector in your town for a payoff figure.

faqs.q: How many municipalities are in Middlesex County?
faqs.a: There are twenty-five. They include Edison, Woodbridge, New Brunswick, East Brunswick, Monroe, Perth Amboy and South Brunswick, and each one runs its own assessment and collection offices.

faqs.q: Can I attend a Middlesex County tax appeal hearing by video?
faqs.a: No. The county board of taxation holds no virtual tax appeal hearings, so plan to attend in person or send your evidence ahead of time.
